## Pythagorean Theorem
Recall that a right triangle has a right angle. Its 2 legs are the sides adjacent to that right angle. The <i>hypotenuse</i> is opposite that right angle.
A common problem solving tool is to build right triangles and using facts about them. The Pythagorean theorem is the 1st, most famous, and most important.

::: {#lem-6.pythag}

<i>Pythagorean theorem</i>: $\triangle ABC$ with side lengths $AB=a$, $BC=b$, and $AC=c$ is a right triangle (with $m \angle B=90^\circ$) if and only if $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

:::

::: {.proof}

"$\to$" Draw the altitude from $B$ to $\overline{AC}$, let point $D$ be its foot. Then $a^2=AD \cdot AC$ and $b^2=CD \cdot AC$ by @lem-5.sim.right, so $a^2+b^2=(AD+CD) \cdot AC=(AC)^2=c^2$.
"$\leftarrow$" Let $\triangle EFG$ be a right triangle with $EF=a$, $FG=b$, and $m \angle F=90^\circ$.
Then $c^2=a^2+b^2=EG^2$, ie $EG=c$ by what we just showed, so $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle EFG$ by SSS congruence @lem-3.sss, so $m \angle B=90^\circ$ by CPCTC and $\triangle ABC$ is a right triangle.

:::

The ancient Egyptians used the Pythagorean Theorem to ensure their bricks, buildings, etc had right angles.
They used a rope split into 12 equal sections that when pulled taut would form a 3-4-5 right triangle.
Math hobbyists have long made a sport of finding more ways to prove the Pythagorean theorem. Many of these involve diagrams/ puzzles, with attributions to Leonardo da Vinci and James A Garfield, among others.

::: {#lem-6.dist}

The <i>distance</i> from a point $A$ to a line $k$ is the length of the shortest segment between the point and the line.<br>
If $A$ is on $k$, the distance is 0. Else (as below, left panel), the distance is $AC$ if and only if $\overline{AC}$ is perpendicular to $k$.<br>
If $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ is parallel to line $k$ (as below, right panel), then points $A,B$ are the same distance from $k$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Part 1: Let $\overline{AC}$ be perpendicular to $k$, $D$ be any point on $k$ besides $C$. Then $\triangle ACD$ is a right triangle with $m \angle ACD=90^\circ$, so $AC^2+CD^2=AD^2$ by the Pythagorean theorem @lem-6.pythag.
Since $D \neq C$, $CD>0$. So $AC^2<AD^2$, and $AC<AD$ since distances are non negative.<br>
Part 2: Let points $C,D$ on $k$ be such that $\overline{AC}, \overline{BD}$ are perpendicular to $k$.
Then $m \angle BAC=m \angle ABD=90^\circ$ by @lem-2.7, so $ABDC$ is a rectangle, so $AC=BD$ by @lem-4.rect.

:::

## 2 special right triangles

::: {#lem-6.45tri}

For $\triangle ABC$, the following are equivalent:

- it is an isosceles right triangle.
- its angles are $45^\circ$, $45^\circ$, and $90^\circ$.
- its side lengths are in ratio $1:1: \sqrt{2}$.

The $\sqrt{2}$ corresponds to the hypotenuse. This triangle is unique up to similarity and is called a <i>45-45-90 triangle</i>.

:::

::: {.proof}

Items 1 and 2 are equivalent by @lem-3.6.isosc and @lem-2.5.
Items 1 and 3 are equivalent, ie we have an isosceles right triangle if and only if the edge lengths are $a, a, a \sqrt{2}$ for some $a>0$ by the Pythagorean theorem @lem-6.pythag.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img = np.ones((500, 500, 3), dtype=np.uint8) * 255
a=(100,100)
b=(400,400)
c=(100,400)
draw_path(img,a,b,c,a)
add_tick(img,a,c)
add_tick(img,b,c)
draw_path(img,(100,380),(120,380),(120,400),thickness=1) #perp marker
cv2.putText(img, "A", (a[0], a[1]-10), font, 0.6, color, 2)
cv2.putText(img, "B", (b[0], b[1]+20), font, 0.6, color, 2)
cv2.putText(img, "C", (c[0], c[1]+20), font, 0.6, color, 2)
cv2.ellipse(img,a,(25,25),0,45,90,color,thickness=1) #angle markers
cv2.ellipse(img,b,(25,25),0,180,225,color,thickness=1)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

Aside: Pythagoras was the head of a secret society whose members were called Pythagoreans.
Among their deeply held beliefs was that all phenomena in nature could be described by whole numbers.
But their study of right triangles inevitably led to irrational numbers, eg for the 45-45-90 triangle, the ratio of lengths of the hypotenuse to either leg is $\sqrt{2}$, which is irrational (proof by contradiction).
It is said that Hippasus was the Pythagorean who pointed out the existence of irrational numbers, and he was murdered as a result.

::: {#lem-6.30tri}

A triangle has angles $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$ if and only if its side lengths are in the ratio $1: \sqrt{3}:2$.
The $30^\circ$ is opposite the side with length 1, and the $90^\circ$ is opposite the side with length 2.<br>
An equilateral triangle with side length $s$ has area $s^2 \sqrt{3}/4$.

:::

Knowing how to derive an equilateral triangle's  area is more important than memorizing its formula.

::: {.proof}

Consider equilateral $\triangle ABC$ with side length $2a>0$. Draw the altitude from point $A$ to $\overline{BC}$, let $M$ be its foot.
Then by @lem-3.6.isosc and @lem-3.6.eqtri, $m \angle B=60^\circ$, $m \angle BAM=30^\circ$, and $BM=a$.
So $AM=a \sqrt{3}$ by the Pythagorean theorem @lem-6.pythag.
Any triangle with side lengths $a, a \sqrt{3}, 2a$ is congruent to $\triangle ABM$ by SSS congruence @lem-3.sss, so its angles must be $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$.<br>
Since $\triangle ABC$ has side length $s=a/2$, by @lem-4.tri.area
$$[ABC]= \frac{BC \cdot AM}{2}= \frac{s \cdot s \sqrt{3}/2}{2}=s^2 \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$$

:::

## Pythagorean triples

A <i>Pythagorean triple</i> is a set of 3 positive integers a,b,c satisfying $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

::: {#exm-6.3.14}

If a,b,c is a Pythagorean triple, then so is na, nb, nc for any positive integer n. (And any real $n>0$ produces valid side lengths for a right triangle)<br>
A geometric proof uses SSS similarity @lem-5.sss. An algebraic proof uses $a^2+b^2=c^2$ if and only if $(na)^2+(nb)^2=(nc)^2$.

:::

::: {#exr-6.3.2}

Let $a, b, c>0$ be a right triangle's side lengths.

- Can they all be odd?
- Can exactly 2 of them be even?
- Can 1 side be an integer, and the other 2 be simple fractions (a ratio of integers, where the denominator is $\geq 2$)?
- Can 1 side be a simple fraction, and the other 2 be integers?

:::

::: {#exm-6.3.15}

If a, b, c is a relatively prime Pythagorean triple, then exactly 1 of them is even, and c is odd. 
Prove that $2mn, m^2-n^2, m^2+n^2$ is a Pythagorean triple for any positive integers $m>n$. (It turns out that any relatively prime Pythagorean triple fits this mold) Find them for $n=1, $m \leq 6$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let a, b, c be a relatively prime Pythagorean triple with a even, and b,c odd. Then $a^2+b^2=c^2$, so $a^2=(c-b)(c+b)$.
Let $m,n>0$ be such that $m^2=(c+b)/2$, $n^2=(c-b)/2$. Then $m^2, n^2$ are integers since b,c are odd. We thus have $a=2mn$, $b=m^2-n^2$, and $c=m^2+n^2$.
From $a^2=4m^2n^2$, and the fact that a, b, c are relatively prime, we see that $m^2, n^2$ are perfect squares, so $m,n$ are in fact integers.

:::

Recognizing Pythagorean triples helps with problem solving to get all of a right triangle's sides without having to compute them via the Pythagorean theorem.
When using Pythagorean triples, make sure that the longest side always corresponds to the hypotenuse, eg a right triangle with legs 5 and 13 does not have hypotenuse 12.<br>
Aside: perhaps inspired by Pythagorean triples, Pierre de Fermat studied the equation $a^n+b^n=c^n$ for integers $n \geq 3$ and postulated that it has no solution using integers a, b, c.
This result is called Fermat's Last Theorem, and was not proven until the 1990s (some 350 years later).

## HL similarity and congruence

Recall from chapter 3 that ssa in general does not imply congruence (and a corresponding result does not imply similarity).
but there is a special case where ssa 'works.'

::: {#lem-6.hl}

<i>Hypotenuse Leg (HL) similarity</i>: Given right triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ with $m \angle C=m \angle F=90^\circ$, if $AB/DE=AC/DF$, then $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$.
<i>HL congruence</i>: if $AB/DE=AC/DF=1$, then $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let $k=AB/DE$. By the Pythagorean theorem @lem-6.pythag, $(EF)^2=(DE)^2-(DF)^2$ and $(BC)^2=(AB)^2-(AC)^2=k^2 \{ (DE)^2-(DF)^2 \}$, so $BC/EF=k$, ie $AB/DE=AC/DF=BC/EF$.
By SSS similarity @lem-5.sss, we have $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$.
If k=1, then by SSS congruence @lem-3.sss, we have $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$.

::: 

```{python}
#| echo: false

b=(250,100)
c=(100,100)
d=(400,100)

draw_path(img,d,e,f,d)

draw_path(img,(380,400),(380,380),(400,380),thickness=1)
for j,lbl in enumerate('ABECFD'):
    p=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=-10 if j%2 else 20
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p[0],p[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

Technically, leg-leg similarity (resp congruence) also holds, but these are just special cases of SAS similarity (resp congruence).

## Heron's Formula\*

Due to SSS congruence, we know a triangle up to congruence given its 3 side lengths, so we should be able to find the area.

::: {#lem-6.heron}

Given a triangle with side lengths $a,b,c>0$, its area is $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$, where $s=(a+b+c)/2$ is the <i>semi perimeter</i>.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let $\triangle ABC$ have $BC=a$, $AC=b$, and $AB=c$. Let $\overline{AP}$ be the altitude from point $A$ to $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ with foot $P$.
Let $x$ denote the 'distance from B to P toward C' (so $x<0$ if P is not on $\overline{BC}$).
Then $(AP)^2=c^2-x^2=b^2-(a-x)^2$ using the Pythagorean theorem @lem-6.pythag twice. We thus have $2ax=c^2+a^2-b^2$.
By @lem-4.tri.area:
$$ \begin{aligned}
\big[ ABC \big]^2=& \frac{a^2}{2^2}(AP)^2= \frac{a^2}{4}\big( c^2-x^2 \big) \\
=& \frac{1}{4}\big\{ (ac)^2- \frac{(c^2+a^2-b^2)^2}{4}\big\} \\
=& \frac{1}{4}\big( ac+ \frac{(c^2+a^2-b^2)^2}{2}\big) \big( ac- \frac{(c^2+a^2-b^2)^2}{2}\big) \\
=& \frac{1}{4}\frac{(c+a)^2-b^2}{2}\frac{(b^2-(c-a)^2}{2}\\
=& \frac{c+a+b}{2}\frac{c+a-b}{2}\frac{b+a-c}{2}\frac{b+c-a}{2}\\
=& s(s-b)(s-c)(s-a)
\end{aligned} $$

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false

p=(200,400)

cv2.putText(img2, "C", (c[0], c[1]+20), font, 0.6, color, 2)
cv2.putText(img2, "P", (p[0], p[1]+20), font, 0.6, color, 2)
show_many_images(img1,img2)
```

While powerful, Heron's formula might not be the optimal way to find a triangle's area given its side lengths.

## Construction: perpendiculars

::: {#exm-6.construct.perp}

Given line k and point A (not on k), construct a line thru A perpendicular to k.<br>
Open the compass enough to construct $\odot A$ to intersect k at 2 points, call them B,C.
Using the same radius, construct $\odot B, \odot C$. They should intersect at point A, let D be the other point of intersection.
Then $\overline{AD}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BC}$.

:::

::: {.proof}

By construction, $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles, with $AB=AC$.
Also by construction and SSS congruence @lem-3.sss, $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACD$. By CPCTC, $\overline{AD}$ bisects $\angle BAC$.
It follows that $\overline{AD}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BC}$ by @lem-3.6.isosc.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img = np.ones((500, 500, 3), dtype=np.uint8) * 255
a=(250,90)
b=(130,250)
c=(370,250)
d=(250,410)
double_arrow_line(img,(50,250),(450,250))
cv2.line(img,a,d,color,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,(250,230),(270,230),(270,250),thickness=1) #perp marker
cv2.ellipse(img,a,(200,200),0,45,135,color,thickness=1)
cv2.ellipse(img,b,(200,200),0,30,75,color,thickness=1)
cv2.ellipse(img,c,(200,200),0,105,150,color,thickness=1)
for j,lbl in enumerate('ACBD'):
    p=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=20 if j%2 else -10
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p[0],p[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'k',(400,240),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.circle(img,a,radius=4,color=color,thickness=-1)
show_geometry_image(img)
```
